newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak trade gap increases in Jan-Oct 1996.
newsitem.headline: Slovak trade gap increases in Jan-Oct 1996.

text.p: The Slovak foreign trade deficit widened in October, spurred by a decline in exports of metal and steel products coupled with a rise in imports of most types of vehicles, but was within analysts' range of forecasts.

The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said on Tuesday the trade gap for the first 10 months of the year widened to 42.52 billion Slovak crowns ($1.37 billion) from 37.17 billion crowns for the January-September period.
Slovakia posted a trade surplus of 18.79 billion crowns for the first 10 months of 1995.
Analysts said the widening of the deficit itself was no reason for concern yet, though some negative fundamentals are behind the trend.
"The development is within the range of our forecast, and we expect the deficit to reach some 52 to 55 billion crowns by the end of this year," said Martin Barto of ING Barings.

"(But) seen from a wider perspective, there are several negative factors behind the (trade) deficit, such as larger consumption-oriented imports and the negative effect of the privatisation process," he added.
The country's main export commodities continued to be iron and rolled steel, accounting for 30.9 billion crowns in the 10 month period but still down 11.3 percent from a year ago.
SUSR said that imports grew 38.5 percent year-on-year for the 10 month period to 266.66 billion crowns, while exports were increased by only 6.1 percent to 224.14 billion crowns.

Imports of fossil fuels and mineral oils totalled about 44 billion crowns, while those for construction of the Mochovce nuclear power plant accounted for another 40.9 billion crowns. Car imports totalled 24.9 billion crowns.
Metal and steel products imports totalled 7.223 billion crowns, while the imports of the airplanes took up 5.855 billion crowns.
Car imports increased year-on-year by 11.3 billion crowns in January-October, while imports of airplanes increased by 4.95 billion crowns, over the same period last year, SUSR said.
Government officials have said the imports consisted mostly of technology necessary for further economic restructuring.
But Barto said this was wishful thinking as imports of consumer goods still accounted for a significant part of overall imports.
Privatisation, which was to have been the first step in restructuring the entire economy, has apparently failed to bring the expected results, he said.
"It seems that some new owners of state property do not use the resources they should be managing to restructure, and just siphon them off for their private benefit," Barto said.

Vladimir Kuklis, an analyst at bank CSOB said it was hard to predict the exact volume of the year-end shortfall, but said his projection was "slightly higher" than the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) forecast of around 52 billion crowns.

Kuklis said he did not expect any dramatic reversal of the current trend in foreign trade in 1997, but added there might be a slight slowdown in the deficit at the beginning of the year. ($1=31.09 Slovak Crown)
